title: Belonging’s Role in Interpreting Ambiguous Feedback
text:
In brief. A professor tells a student, “This is a difficult major, many students do not persevere and instead drop out to study something easier.” Is that a warning or a vote of confidence? I ran three online studies (N = 1,125) in which students imagined hearing exactly that in office hours, then rated it, wrote about it, and used that feedback to pick next semester’s classes. Study 1 was exploratory, examining general trends in how students interpret academic feedback. Based on the findings from Study 1, Study 2 preregistered specific success criteria and replicated Study 1’s findings. Study 3 then extended the findings to test their robustness. Men read the comment more positively than women in all three studies; students who felt they belonged socially in their major read it more positively in two of the three. And students who read it more positively subsequently reported using the feedback to pursue harder, more rewarding classes.

title: Belonging’s Role in Interpreting Ambiguous Feedback
text:
The problem
Research recommends feedback that is specific and actionable. Much of what people actually hear, however, is a passing remark that requires the feedback recipient to fill in their own meaning. Earlier work had found that men and women read explicitly negative feedback differently; however, almost nobody has tested the murky middle of ambiguous feedback, where most real feedback occurs. The same question comes up whenever an organization speaks to people in a sentence that could go either way (e.g. a status that reads “under review,” an error message, a policy notice).

title: Belonging’s Role in Interpreting Ambiguous Feedback
text:
What I did
Study 1, exploratory (n = 423). Participants read the scenario and rated the comment on four items (how positive it was, how confident the professor seemed in them, how they felt afterward, and whether they would go back for more feedback). They then chose between a difficult-but-fulfilling class and two easy ones, and completed scales for social belonging (feeling part of the major’s community) and intellectual belonging (confidence in their own ability). I used a program of model comparison to identify the clearest relationships between variables, which became the hypotheses for Study 2.
Study 2, preregistered direct replication (n = 233). Same materials. Before collecting data I preregistered the hypotheses, a power analysis (at least 200 participants for .80 power), the exclusion rules, and what would count as success: each estimate had to land within one standard error of Study 1’s, and the model’s R² between .03 and .10. All exploratory findings from Study 1 (feedback interpretation differed by gender and social belonging) replicated in this model.






Preregistration



Preregistration means writing down your predictions, your sample size, and what will count as success before collecting any data, then posting it publicly with a timestamp. It keeps a researcher from moving the goalposts after seeing the results. It is the same reason a product team should decide what counts as a win before an A/B test starts.


Study 3, preregistered extension (n = 469). Expanded on Studies 1 and 2. Participants reported the grade they believed would earn them the ambiguous feedback as well as their real standing in the major. They also wrote about the conversation in their own words. Three research assistants coded every paragraph for how the writer saw themselves, the professor, and the interaction (inter-rater α = .76 to .88), and a sentiment analysis scored the three-word answers for positive and negative emotionality.
All three studies ran in Qualtrics under IRB approval.

What came out

"inside" : "outside"}`})
  ]
})























Each dot is one study’s estimate with its 95% interval. The gold band is the success range set from Study 1 and written into the preregistration before Studies 2 and 3 were run. A filled dot landed inside it; an open dot did not. Left: how much more positively men rated the comment than women, on a 1 to 5 scale. Right: the change in rating for each point of social belonging. Hover for the numbers.







Reading this chart



Before running Studies 2 and 3, I wrote down how big each effect had to be to count as a successful repeat of Study 1; that is the gold band. Each dot is what a study actually found, and the line through it is the range of plausible values. For gender, all three dots landed in the band, so the finding held up every time. For social belonging, the third study came in below the band, so that finding is less certain.


Gender replicated cleanly. Men rated the comment more positively than women in every study, by about 0.4 points on a five-point scale (average ratings of 2.09 to 2.60 for women and 2.52 to 3.04 for men), and all three estimates landed inside the preregistered range. The gap held after controlling for academic standing and for major (STEM, psychology, or other), which rules out the simplest explanation, that men just believed they were doing better.
Belonging replicated with caveats. Social belonging predicted a more positive reading in Studies 1 and 2, and Study 2’s estimate landed inside its range. In Study 3 the effect pointed the same way but was too small to meet the criterion. Study 3 ran in fall 2020, for many participants a first term spent entirely online, which may have changed what belonging to a major even meant. Intellectual belonging never predicted how the comment was read, although men reported more of it.
The open-text answers told a more detailed version of the same story. In their paragraphs, men described themselves and the interaction more positively than women did, and in their three-word answers they used fewer negative words for how they felt. However, men and women did not describe the professor any differently.

Feedback perception predicted subsequent class choices. Students who read the comment more positively leaned toward the difficult-but-fulfilling class (controlling for gender), in Studies 1 and 3 (Study 2 pointed the same way but was not significant). In Study 3, part of the gender gap in class choice ran through how the feedback was interpreted (indirect effect b = 0.07, 95% CI 0.02 to 0.14).






What an “indirect effect” means



Women were less likely than men to say they would take the harder class. Part of the reason ran through the feedback itself: women read the comment more negatively, and students who read it more negatively were less drawn to the harder class. The indirect effect measures how much of the gender gap travels along that path. It is small, but it suggests a single ambiguous sentence can nudge a real decision.

title: Belonging’s Role in Interpreting Ambiguous Feedback
text:
What this is good for
When wording is ambiguous, readers supply the meaning, and different groups of readers supply it differently and predictably. These effects are compounded when feedback is read without vocal tone or other interpersonal cues. For anyone who writes the sentences people see in a portal, a letter, or an app, a message has to be tested on the people who will actually read it.

Email  GitHub  LinkedIn  Scholar  Résumé


How does what we say reflect how we understand each other and ourselves?
I’m a behavioral scientist and data scientist who has spent seven years studying this question. My work brings together a wide array of tools from natural language processing to Bayesian statistics to experimental and survey design. Across all of my projects, I’m guided by three principles:
1) Quality measurement. Are we actually measuring the thing that we think we’re measuring?

2) Replicability. Do our findings tell us about the wider world or do they only tell us about the specific people we surveyed?

3) Accessible scientific communication. Can non-scientists understand what we found, how we found it, and why it matters?
If I’m not wrangling data at my desk, I’m deep in the woods with my dog.

title: Which Parts of a Conversation Reveal What Someone Is Thinking?
text:
In brief. When you try to work out what someone is thinking, which of their words should you pay attention to? I combined six studies, recorded over roughly 20 years, in which people watched recorded conversations and wrote down what they thought a speaker was thinking; the speakers had also written down what they were actually thinking. I transcribed 74 hours of video, labeled each unique utterance as a dialogue act (e.g., question, suggestion, statement, and so on), and measured how closely each one matched the guesser’s guesses and the speaker’s real thoughts. Three results emerged: Suggestions matched what speakers were thinking more closely, on average, than any other kind of utterance, questions included. The most recent words carried the most information. And it made no difference whether those words came from the speaker or from their conversation partner.

title: Which Parts of a Conversation Reveal What Someone Is Thinking?
text:
The question
Earlier research showed that people read each other more accurately when they can hear what is said. It had not asked which words, said when, and by whom. Research on conversation also treats questions as the best way to draw out what someone is thinking (Graesser & Person, 1994), so I expected questions to be the most revealing.

title: Which Parts of a Conversation Reveal What Someone Is Thinking?
text:
What I did
Turned video into text. I used a transcription model (Whisper) to transcribe the videos and coached a team of 15 research assistants to review transcriptions for accuracy I then hand-coded 5,000 utterances to train a model that split speech into single utterances; on a holdout sample utterances it had never seen, it agreed with human coding with 96.8% accuracy.
Labeled every utterance. I used a set of four language models to vote on whether each utterance was a question, suggestion, statement, agreement etc. The combined vote matched human coding 93.4% of the time, better than any published single model on this task.
Measured how close two sentences are. Every utterance, guess, and thought was converted into a sentence embedding so I could score how similar any two were in meaning.






How a computer compares two sentences



A sentence embedding turns a sentence into a long list of numbers that captures its meaning. “I’m nervous about the exam” and “this test is stressing me out” don’t share any words, but their lists of numbers end up close together because the underlying meaning is similar. Comparing two using the cosine of the angle between the vector of numbers gives a similarity score ranging from -1 to +1 where higher means closer in meaning. That let me ask, for every single utterance, how close it came to what the speaker was actually thinking.


Modeled change over time. Bayesian models traced how similarity rose and fell over the course of each conversation, one study at a time, and then combined all six studies into a single estimate.






Note



74 hours of video, 1,346 observers, 956 speakers, and 11,906 written guesses. Transcripts are IRB-restricted and stay in the lab; this page shows model summaries only.

title: Which Parts of a Conversation Reveal What Someone Is Thinking?
Which Parts of a Conversation Reveal What Someone Is Thinking?
text:
What this is good for
The same pipeline can be easily adapted to run on user interviews, support calls, or sales calls. For user research, the suggestions result is also a practical one. Analysis usually focuses on how people answer the questions we ask them. However, there are contexts when someone may volunteers a proposal (“it would be easier if…”) outside of an interview that may say more about what they are thinking.

title: How Liberals and Conservatives Talk About Cancel Culture
How Liberals and Conservatives Talk About Cancel Culture
text:
The question
“Cancel culture” gets invoked with a great deal of confidence and very little data. Underneath the argument are two questions any organization that listens to the public has to answer: who is talking, and how are different groups framing the same thing?

title: How Liberals and Conservatives Talk About Cancel Culture
text:
What I did
Estimated political lean from profile bios. A small share of users (1 to 9%) state their politics outright in their bio with terms like “#BlueWave” or “GOP.” I used them as anchors, then scored every other bio word by how closely it tracks those anchors across the millions of bios. That produced a usable estimate of partisan lean for between a third and a half of all users.






Reading politics from a bio



Picture a bio that reads “dog mom, nurse, #BlueWave.” The hashtag gives a clear clue to her political leaning. The more interesting part, however, is that “dog mom” and “nurse” now carry a little information too. Over millions of bios, non-political words get associated with clear liberal or conservative signals (or get associated with other words that are associated with clear partisan terms). Add up those small signals across a whole bio and you get a rough estimate of lean for people, even if they never mention politics.


Scored moral and emotional language. I measured moral language with a published dictionary of moral words and checked it against two AI models trained to recognize similar categories. I then built an outrage score from dictionary terms for harm, cheating, betrayal, subversion, and degradation, and ran separate AI classifiers for anger, sentiment, and irony to check it.
Tracked time. For 23 cancellations with a verifiable date for the behavior itself (the tweet, remark, or incident, not the news coverage or a firing), I lined up each person’s tweets by that date and followed the outrage score for a month afterward.
Modeled topics. Using a variant of latent Dirichlet allocation, I identified different topics that were discussed by the different political groups (e.g., “mob justice”).






Note



8,572,185 English-language tweets from 4,035,488 users, collected in late 2022 through Twitter’s research API. Platform terms prohibit sharing tweet or bio text, so everything here is an aggregate. Code: github.com/zjschroeder/Cancel-Culture-Text-Analysis.

title: How Liberals and Conservatives Talk About Cancel Culture
text:
What I found
Liberal and conservative users brought different moral lenses to the same events. Each cell below compares how often conservative- and liberal-leaning users used one kind of moral language in one sample.

ml = FileAttachment("data/moral_by_lean.csv").csv({typed: true})
foundations = ["care", "harm", "fairness", "cheating", "loyalty", "betrayal", "authority", "subversion", "sanctity", "degradation", "outrage_proxy"]
foundLabel = new Map([["care", "Care"], ["harm", "Harm"], ["fairness", "Fairness"], ["cheating", "Cheating"], ["loyalty", "Loyalty"], ["betrayal", "Betrayal"], ["authority", "Authority"], ["subversion", "Subversion"], ["sanctity", "Sanctity"], ["degradation", "Degradation"], ["outrage_proxy", "Outrage"]])
studies = ["Cancel Culture", "Is Over Party", "Academics", "Celebrities", "Civilians"]
// ratio = conservative rate / liberal rate; log2 so that 2x and 1/2x sit equally far from "same"
ratio = studies.flatMap(s => {
  const con = ml.find(d => d.study === s && d.lean === "Conservative");
  const lib = ml.find(d => d.study === s && d.lean === "Liberal");
  return foundations.map(f => ({study: s, foundation: foundLabel.get(f), con: con[f], lib: lib[f], log2ratio: Math.log2(con[f] / lib[f])}));
})
gapLabel = d => {
  const r = Math.pow(2, d.log2ratio);
  if (r > 0.95 && r < 1.05) return "same";
  return r > 1 ? `${r.toFixed(1)}× con` : `${(1 / r).toFixed(1)}× lib`;
}
Plot.plot({
  width: 760, height: 310, marginLeft: 110, marginBottom: 60,
  x: {label: null, domain: foundations.map(f => foundLabel.get(f)), tickRotate: -30},
  y: {label: null, domain: studies},
  color: {type: "diverging", scheme: "RdBu", reverse: true, domain: [-1.3, 1.3], legend: true, width: 400,
    label: "Which side used this kind of language more",
    ticks: [-1, 0, 1],
    tickFormat: d => d === 0 ? "same" : d > 0 ? `${Math.pow(2, d).toFixed(1)}× con` : `${Math.pow(2, -d).toFixed(1)}× lib`},
  marks: [
    Plot.cell(ratio, {x: "foundation", y: "study", fill: "log2ratio", inset: 1, tip: true,
      title: d => `${d.study}, ${d.foundation}\nconservative-leaning users: ${(d.con * 1000).toFixed(1)} per 1,000 words\nliberal-leaning users: ${(d.lib * 1000).toFixed(1)} per 1,000 words\n${gapLabel(d) === "same" ? "about the same" : gapLabel(d).endsWith("con") ? `conservatives used it ${gapLabel(d).split("×")[0]} times as often` : `liberals used it ${gapLabel(d).split("×")[0]} times as often`}`}),
    Plot.text(ratio, {x: "foundation", y: "study", text: gapLabel, fill: d => Math.abs(d.log2ratio) > 0.6 ? "white" : "#111", fontSize: 10})
  ]
})



















































Red cells: conservative-leaning users used that kind of language more. Blue cells: liberal-leaning users did. The label says how many times as often (“2.1× con” means conservatives used it 2.1 times as often as liberals). Hover for the underlying rates.







Reading the heatmap



Each cell compares one kind of moral language between the two groups. The label tells you which group used it more and by how much: “2.1× con” means conservative-leaning users used it 2.1 times as often as liberal-leaning users, and “2.1× lib” means the reverse. The color says the same thing, red for conservative and blue for liberal, and the deeper the color, the bigger the gap. For example, when academics were canceled, conservatives used fairness language 2.1 times as often as liberals did; when celebrities were canceled, liberals used sanctity (purity) language 2.1 times as often as conservatives did.


Fairness showed the biggest gap, but its direction depended on who was being canceled: conservatives used it far more when the target was an academic or a private citizen, and slightly less in the other samples. Betrayal, degradation, and outrage leaned conservative in most samples.
They also talked about different parts of the story. Conservative-leaning users spent more of their tweets on free speech and on the idea of “the mob”; liberal-leaning users spent more on accountability and consequences. Although gaps are a few percentage points, for a dataset of millions of tweets, that marks a sizable difference in conversations.
Outrage arrived with the attention, then lingered.

  ]

Day 0 is the date of the behavior itself (the tweet, remark, video, or incident), found by searching news coverage for each of the 23 cases listed below. Each point averages that day and up to six days before it, counting only days from day 0 on. Days before day 0 are left off: most people in the sample were barely tweeted about before their behavior, so those averages rest on a handful of people. The academic jump around day 15 comes mostly from one case whose remarks went viral about two weeks after they aired.







The 23 cancellations in this figure






cancelEvents = FileAttachment("data/cancellation_events.csv").csv({typed: false})
Inputs.table(cancelEvents, {
  columns: ["type", "person", "event_date", "event", "consequence_date", "consequence", "source"],
  header: {type: "Group", person: "Person", event_date: "Day 0", event: "What happened", consequence_date: "Later action", consequence: "What the institution did", source: "Source"},
  format: {source: d => d ? htl.html`<a href=${d} target="_blank">link</a>` : ""},
  width: {type: 90, person: 130, event_date: 90, consequence_date: 90, source: 50},
  rows: 14, sort: "event_date"
})















Day 0 is the date of the behavior itself, not when news covered it or when an employer acted; later actions are listed separately. Dates marked ±1 day in the data file could only be pinned that closely. Cases were left out when the behavior could not be dated to the day (for example, years-old tweets that resurfaced, or remarks recorded at an unknown time), when the only available date was news coverage or a firing, or when the dataset held fewer than 20 tweets within a month of the behavior.









Lining up the timelines



Every cancellation happened on a different date, so I looked up the date of each person’s behavior (the tweet, the remark, the incident) and reset their clock: day 0 is that date. Averaging the reset timelines shows the typical arc. For celebrities, outrage jumped from about 3 outrage words per 1,000 in the month before (not shown) to about 10 within two days, as attention peaked, and stayed near that level for the rest of the month even as the number of tweets fell by more than 90%. Civilians held steady at about 8 from the first day. The academic line is less certain because it rests on five to eight people. Its jump around day 15 is mostly one case: Amy Wax’s podcast remarks aired on day 0 but were not widely noticed until about two weeks later, a reminder that the behavior and the outrage are not always close together.


An anger score is not an outrage score. An off-the-shelf AI “anger” classifier and the moral-outrage measure were essentially unrelated (r = −.05). As such, building a unique measure of outrage allowed me to specify the type and context of the negative emotionality.

title: How Liberals and Conservatives Talk About Cancel Culture
text:
What this is good for
Interviews and surveys capture what people say when a researcher asks. A dataset like this captures what they say to each other. The same approach would work on support tickets, portal comments, or reviews: estimate who is talking, compare how each group frames the same event, and watch how the tone shifts in the days after something goes wrong.
